title: Venezuela's Acting President Just Landed in Delhi. India's Oil Crisis Brought Her Here.
excerpt: Delcy Rodriguez's five-day visit coincides with India importing 427,000 barrels a day of Venezuelan crude — the most since 2020 — as the Hormuz blockade forces New Delhi to look west.
body:
Venezuela's acting President Delcy Rodriguez arrived in New Delhi on Wednesday for a five-day visit that puts India's deepening energy crisis at the centre of a diplomatic relationship that barely existed a year ago.

The visit, from June 3 to 7, will include bilateral talks with Prime Minister Narendra Modi and meetings with India's top energy industry leaders in Mumbai. Rodriguez is accompanied by ministers responsible for foreign affairs, economy and finance, science and technology, communication, and transportation — a delegation calibrated more for deal-making than ceremony.

## The Numbers Tell the Story

India was the second-largest importer of Venezuelan crude in May, purchasing 427,000 barrels per day, behind only the United States. In April, shipments had climbed to 283,000 barrels per day, the highest since March 2020, according to data from Kpler. The analytics firm estimates June arrivals could rise further to 380,000 barrels per day.

A year ago, India was not buying Venezuelan oil at all. President Trump had authorised a 25 percent discretionary tariff on countries purchasing crude from Caracas. That changed in February, when Washington eased sanctions following a supply pact reached after the US detention of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January. Under the agreement, the US Treasury controls proceeds from Venezuelan oil sales, a concession that made the trade politically palatable.

Reliance Industries, controlled by Mukesh Ambani, has been among the largest buyers. The company signed a term agreement in 2012 to source up to 400,000 barrels per day from Petroleos de Venezuela SA and is one of the few Indian refiners capable of processing Venezuela's heavy, high-sulphur crude.

## Why It Matters for India

The urgency is straightforward. The US-Israeli war on Iran, which began on February 28, has effectively shut the Strait of Hormuz — a chokepoint that carried more than 40 percent of India's crude oil imports before the conflict. India imports roughly 90 percent of the crude it consumes, making the disruption existential for its economy.

With Iranian oil largely inaccessible and Middle Eastern routes under threat, India has been forced to diversify at speed. Venezuela, along with increased purchases from Russia, West Africa and the US itself, has become a critical piece of that puzzle. But analysts caution against over-reliance.

"Venezuela has the potential to become a longer-term supplier to India, particularly as refiners seek cost-competitive alternatives to Middle Eastern grades," said Sumit Ritolia, modelling and refining manager at Kpler. "However, Venezuelan production remains relatively constrained and is unlikely to materially alter India's overall import requirements."

## The Diaspora Dimension

For Indians in the US and the Gulf, the visit carries a dual significance. The same sanctions relaxation that allows Indian refiners to buy Venezuelan crude is also being watched by Indian energy sector workers in Houston and the broader diaspora, many of whom work in the oil and gas industry and understand how fragile these supply chains have become.

Rodriguez's agenda extends beyond oil. Discussions will cover pharmaceuticals, healthcare, transportation and renewable energy — sectors where Indian companies have made significant investments in Venezuela. Indian public sector undertakings have had a presence in Venezuela's energy sector for years and are now exploring opportunities to expand.

This is Rodriguez's sixth visit to India. She previously came as Venezuela's foreign minister in 2015, as vice president in 2019, 2023, 2024 and 2025, and most recently as oil minister at India Energy Week in February 2025. The frequency tells its own story: India and Venezuela are building something more durable than an emergency workaround, even if the emergency is what brought them to the table.
author: Diaspora Desk
